# 1 Introduction

# 2 Loading the R package

In this exercise, the following packages are used:

tidyverse – A collection of data science packages (readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, etc.) with a unified grammar for importing, wrangling, and visualising data.

sf – Simple Features for R: create, read, write, transform, and analyse vector geospatial data (points/lines/polygons) with modern CRS support.

sfdep – Provides functions for spatial dependence analysis, including tools for computing spatial weights, spatial autocorrelation measures, and emerging hotspot analysis, extending the functionality of the sf package.

tmap – A flexible thematic mapping package that supports both static and interactive maps.

knitr – An engine for dynamic report generation, allowing integration of R code and results into documents.

kableExtra – Extends knitr::kable() by providing advanced table styling features. It allows users to create publication-quality tables in HTML and LaTeX.

DT – An R interface to the DataTables JavaScript library, enabling interactive tables with features such as searching, filtering, sorting, and pagination.

Kendall – Implements the Mann-Kendall trend test and related functions for detecting monotonic trends in time series data.

scales – Provides tools for scaling data and controlling axis, legend, and color breaks in visualisations.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, sfdep, tmap, knitr, kableExtra, DT, Kendall, scales)
```
:::


# 3 Data Importing and Wrangling

## Importing Data

The following datasets are imported:

- Bus Stop Location shapefile downloaded from LTA DataMall

- Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) from Singapore’s open data portal

- Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops downloaded from LTA DataMall


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
#Bus Stop Location
BusStop = st_read(dsn = "data/LTADataMall/", 
                  layer = "BusStop") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

## Extracting Bus Stops located within Singapore

The code below assigns each bus stop to the planning subzone it belongs to, creating a dataset of bus stops (BusStop_in_SG) linked to their respective subzones.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz, 
  join = st_within, 
  left = FALSE)
```
:::


### Visualize

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons() +
tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) +
  tm_dots()
```

## Deriving Analytical Hexagon

The code below generates a hexagonal tessellation over Singapore’s planning subzones to standardize spatial units for analysis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz, 
                        cellsize = 750,
                        what = "polygon",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()
```
:::


## Selecting hexagons with bus stops

The code below links bus stops to the analytical hexagons, counts how many fall inside each, and filters the grid to include only meaningful hexagons with bus stops.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon$busstop_count =
  lengths(st_intersects(
    hexagon, BusStop_in_SG))

hexagon <- filter(
  hexagon, busstop_count > 0)
```
:::


## Assigning ids to each hexagon

The code below cleans the hexagon dataset by dropping the temporary count column and assigns each hexagon a unique identifier (HEX_ID) for consistent reference in spatial analysis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon <- hexagon %>% 
  select(, -busstop_count)

hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf(
  "H%04d", seq_len(
    nrow(hexagon))) %>% 
  as.factor()
```
:::


## Preparing Trip Generation Data

The code below extracts the relevant bus trip information, standardizes the column names into intuitive labels (BUS_STOP_N, HOUR_OF_DAY, TRIPS), and prepares the bus stop IDs as categorical values for later aggregation and spatial analysis.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trips <- odbus %>%
  select(c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>%
  rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>%
  rename(HOUR_OF_DAY = TIME_PER_HOUR) %>%
  rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS)
trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N)
```
:::


## Populating Hexagon IDs into BusStop data frame

The code below creates a lookup table that links each bus stop to the hexagon it belongs to. It is essential for aggregating bus trips at the hexagon level later on.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
bs_hex <- st_intersection(
  BusStop, hexagon) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID))
```
:::


## Adding HEX_ID into bus trips data

The code below enriches the trip dataset by adding hexagon IDs to each bus trip record, enabling aggregation and spatial analysis of trips at the hexagon level.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trips <- inner_join(trips, bs_hex)
```
:::


## Aggregating TRIPS based on HEX_ID

The code below converts raw trip records into spatial-temporal summaries, making the data easier to analyze by hexagon location, type of day, and hour of day.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trips <- trips %>%
  group_by(
    HEX_ID,
    DAY_TYPE,
    HOUR_OF_DAY) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS))
```
:::



# 4 Weekday morning peak

## 4.1 Overview

### Choropleth map of total trips


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
weekday_morning <- trips %>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", HOUR_OF_DAY %in% 6:9) %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(hexagon, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  st_as_sf()

tmap_mode("plot")

tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +
  
  tm_shape(weekday_morning) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "TRIPS",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "quantile",  # Use style = "quantile" instead
      n = 5,
      values = "viridis"
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "Total Trips\n(Weekday Morning)",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
    )
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Bus Trips - Weekday Morning Peak (6am-9am)") +
  tm_compass(position = tm_pos_in("left", "top")) +
  tm_scale_bar(position = tm_pos_in("left", "bottom"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TakeHome_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The visualisation shows that bus trips during the weekday morning peak (6–9am) are heavily concentrated in large residential towns such as Tampines, Pasir Ris, Yishun, and Woodlands, as well as the western corridor around Jurong East and Clementi. Moderate activity is seen in areas like Hougang, Sengkang, and Punggol, while peripheral industrial and coastal zones record low trip counts. Overall, the map highlights a polycentric commuting pattern, where dense housing estates generate significant trips feeding into central employment areas, reinforcing the key role of buses in connecting residential towns with work and study destinations.

The histogram of trip counts during the weekday morning peak (6–9am) shows a clear right-skewed distribution, where most hexagons generate relatively few trips and only a small number experience very high volumes. The median trip count is 14,934, while the mean is 30,884, reflecting the influence of extreme outliers. The 95th percentile is much higher at 110,640 trips, with a few hexagons exceeding even this threshold, reaching nearly 400,000 trips. This indicates that while the majority of areas have modest bus activity, a small set of high-demand locations—likely major housing estates or transport hubs—contribute disproportionately to overall flows. The skew highlights an uneven distribution of bus demand, with most places generating low-to-moderate trips, but a few nodes acting as critical centers of commuter activity.

## 4.2 Local Indicators of Spatial Association(LISA)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
critical_dist <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(weekday_morning))

nb <- st_dist_band(
  st_geometry(weekday_morning),
  upper = critical_dist)

n_neighbors <- lengths(nb)

wt <- st_weights(nb, style = "W")

# Compute Local Moran's I
set.seed(1234)
lisa_morning <- weekday_morning %>%
  mutate(
    local_moran = local_moran(
      TRIPS, nb, wt, nsim = 99), 
    .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(local_moran)
```
:::


### Local Moran’s I values and p-values


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ii_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +  # base layer

  tm_shape(lisa_morning) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.RdBu"
              ),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Local Moran's I",
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                title.size = 0.7,        # Smaller title
                text.size = 0.6,
              )
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I - morning peak")

p_ii_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +

  tm_shape(lisa_morning) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, Inf),
                values = "-brewer.Reds"
              ),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "p-value",
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")
              )
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("p-values of Local Moran's I")

tmap_arrange(ii_map, p_ii_map, asp = 1, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TakeHome_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The Local Moran's I geovisualisation for the weekday morning peak reveals strong spatial clustering of bus trip activity across Singapore.

The left map shows medium to dark blue areas (2 to 5) identifying High-High clusters concentrated in central, northeastern, northern, and western regions including towns like Tampines, Punggol, Yishun, Woodlands, Jurong, and the CBD corridor. These represent significant commuter hotspots where high trip counts are surrounded by similarly high-demand hexagons, reflecting major residential-to-workplace flows during morning peak hours. Light orange shades (-1 to 0) highlight weak clustering or spatial outliers in peripheral and industrial zones where trip patterns diverge from neighbors. The right map confirms statistical robustness through p-values. Dark red shades (p < 0.001 to 0.01) concentrated across central, northern, northeastern, and western Singapore demonstrate that clustering is highly significant and systematic, not random. Pale areas (p > 0.05) indicate dispersed patterns in low-density zones.

Overall, the analysis reveals strong positive spatial autocorrelation with concentrated morning demand hotspots aligned with major commuter corridors, residential estates, and transit hubs, confirming systematic workplace-bound travel patterns during the weekday morning peak.

### Moran scatterplot with standardised variable

```{.r .cell-code}
  mutate(lag_TRIPS = st_lag(

    .before = 1) %>%

lisa_morning <- lisa_morning %>%
  mutate(z_TRIPS = scale(TRIPS),
         z_lag_TRIPS = scale(lag_TRIPS),
         .before = 1)

ggplot(data = lisa_morning,
       aes(x = z_TRIPS,
           y = z_lag_TRIPS,
           color = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm",
              se = FALSE,
              color = "black") +

  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(lisa_morning$z_TRIPS), lty = 2) +

    values = c("High-High" = "red",
               "Low-Low" = "blue",
               "Low-High" = "lightblue",
               "High-Low" = "pink")) +

```

The High-High quadrant (red, upper right) contains numerous points representing hexagons with high trip counts surrounded by similarly high-trip neighbors, forming significant positive spatial autocorrelation clusters in dense residential and employment zones with strong commuting demand. The Low-Low quadrant (dark blue, lower left) shows cold spots where low-trip hexagons cluster together, typically in peripheral or less populated regions, also exhibiting positive spatial autocorrelation.

The High-Low quadrant (pink, lower right) contains few points representing spatial outliers—isolated high-trip hexagons surrounded by low-trip areas, suggesting unique transit hubs or stations. The Low-High quadrant (light blue, upper left) shows underperforming hexagons within busier regions, indicating negative spatial autocorrelation outliers.
The positive slope of the regression line confirms overall positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning similar trip intensities cluster together systematically.

In summary, the scatterplot validates that weekday morning bus trips exhibit strong positive spatial dependence, with pronounced hotspot and coldspot clustering and minimal outliers.

The LISA map for weekday morning peak reveals clear clusters of significant spatial autocorrelation in bus trip volumes across Singapore. High-High clusters (in red) appear prominently in the central and eastern regions, including dense residential and mixed-use areas, indicating concentrations of high trip volumes surrounded by other high-volume hexagons. These represent strong hotspots of demand during the morning peak. Conversely, Low-Low clusters (in dark blue) are mostly located in the western and peripheral regions, where low trip counts are surrounded by other low-volume areas, reflecting weaker bus demand in suburban or less connected zones.

Notably, some Low-High and High-Low outliers (in light blue and pink) emerge along the boundaries of clusters, suggesting transitional zones where high-demand cells are adjacent to low-demand cells and vice versa. The presence of these outliers indicates local heterogeneity and the influence of bordering subzones. Overall, the spatial patterns confirm that bus trips are not randomly distributed but exhibit strong clustering aligned with Singapore’s urban structure, with demand hotspots concentrated in central/eastern hubs and cold spots at the urban periphery.

## 4.3 Hot Spots and Cold Spots Analysis (HCSA)

### Gi* values and p-values


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Compute fixed distance weight matrix
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(weekday_morning))

weekday_morning_fdw <- weekday_morning %>%
  mutate(nb = include_self(
    st_dist_band(
      st_geometry(geometry),
      upper = ct)),
    wt = st_weights(nb,
                    style = "W"),
    .before = 1)

# Compute local Gi*

set.seed(1234)

HCSA_fdw <- weekday_morning_fdw %>%
  mutate(
    gistar = local_gstar_perm(
      TRIPS, nb, wt, nsim = 99),
    .before = 1) %>%
  unnest(gistar)

# Plot Gi* values
Gi_star_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +
  
  tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "gi_star",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "pretty",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "local Gi*",
                position = tm_pos_in(
                  "right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Local Gi* of TRIPS")

# Plot p-values
p_values_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +
  
  tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_sim",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 1),
                values = "-brewer.reds"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "p-value",
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("p-values of local Gi* of TRIPS")

# Display both maps side by side
tmap_arrange(Gi_star_map, p_values_map, asp = 1, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](TakeHome_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


The Local Gi* map (left) highlights concentrated hotspots in central and eastern regions, shown in red, where bus trip intensity is significantly higher than expected. Conversely, coldspots appear in the west and northwest, marked in blue, where trip counts are consistently lower relative to their neighbours. This contrast reflects commuting dynamics, with central and eastern hubs acting as major destinations.

The p-value map (right) supports the robustness of these patterns. Many hotspots and coldspots overlap with areas of low p-values (<0.05, dark red shades), confirming their statistical significance and suggesting that the clustering is unlikely to be due to random variation. Meanwhile, lighter shades (higher p-values) indicate regions where clustering is weaker or not statistically reliable.

### HCSA Map


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# HCSA cluster classification
HCSA_fdw <- HCSA_fdw %>%
  mutate(HCSA_cluster = case_when(
    p_sim > 0.05 ~ "Insignificant",
    p_sim <= 0.05 & cluster == "High" ~ "Hot spot",
    p_sim <= 0.05 & cluster == "Low" ~ "Cold spot",
    TRUE ~ "Other"),
    HCSA_cluster = factor(
      HCSA_cluster,
      levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
    ),
    .before = 1
  )

# Plot HCSA cluster map
HCSA_map <- tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "grey90", border.col = "white") +
  
  tm_shape(HCSA_fdw) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "HCSA_cluster",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
      values = c(
        "grey80",  # Insignificant
        "red",     # Hot spot
        "blue"     # Cold spot
      )
    ),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      title = "HCSA Cluster",
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"))
  ) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_title("HCSA Clusters (p < 0.05)")

# Gi* map and HCSA map
tmap_arrange(Gi_star_map, HCSA_map, asp = 1, ncol = 2)
```

The right-hand map, showing Hot Spot and Cold Spot Analysis (HCSA) clusters, highlights statistically significant spatial clusters of bus trips during the weekday morning peak (6–9am). Red areas represent hot spots, where hexagons with high trip counts are surrounded by other high trip hexagons. These are concentrated in central and eastern Singapore, indicating consistently high demand in dense urban and employment hubs. Blue areas represent cold spots, where low trip counts cluster together, and these are more evident in peripheral regions such as the western and north-western areas. Grey areas indicate insignificant clusters, where trip patterns do not form clear spatial groupings. This contrast emphasizes that bus trip demand is not evenly distributed but spatially clustered: strong activity occurs in central commuting corridors and urban nodes, while peripheral regions consistently experience low demand.

Together, the two maps complement each other: the Local Gi* shows where clustering intensity is strongest, while the HCSA map strengthens interpretation by focusing only on statistically robust clusters.

## 4.4 Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hex_ids <- hexagon$HEX_ID

trips_morning_hourly <- trips %>%
  filter(DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY", HOUR_OF_DAY %in% 5:10) %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>%
  summarise(TRIPS = sum(TRIPS), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::complete(HEX_ID = hex_ids, HOUR_OF_DAY = 5:10,
                  fill = list(TRIPS = 0)) %>%
  arrange(HEX_ID, HOUR_OF_DAY)

trips_morning_hourly$HEX_ID <- factor(trips_morning_hourly$HEX_ID, levels = hex_ids)
trips_morning_hourly$HOUR_OF_DAY <- as.integer(trips_morning_hourly$HOUR_OF_DAY)

# Build space–time cube
TRIPS_morning_st <- spacetime(
  trips_morning_hourly,
  hexagon %>% select(HEX_ID), 
  .loc_col  = "HEX_ID",
  .time_col = "HOUR_OF_DAY"
)

is_spacetime_cube(TRIPS_morning_st) 
```
